title: Paediatric basic life support and choking (RCUK 2025)
blurb: Deliver paediatric basic life support to RCUK 2025, from 5 rescue breaths to the right compression ratio and AED mode, and manage a choking infant or child.
question: A community children's nurse trained in paediatric basic life support finds Ivy, 4 months, unresponsive and not breathing normally at home. Her mother has called the ambulance on speaker phone. What should the nurse do next?

teach.h: Why children need their own algorithm
teach.body: Most children who arrest do so because of breathing or circulatory failure, not a primary heart problem, so they are usually hypoxic first. That is why paediatric BLS starts with 5 rescue breaths. Formally, the RCUK 2025 paediatric guidelines apply from birth to 18 years; if a rescuer believes the person is an adult, they use the adult algorithm. Plain English: oxygen first, then compressions, and do not delay for an AED if you are alone.
teach.cite: RCUK 2025 Paediatric basic life support (27 Oct 2025)

steps.label: Safety
steps.sub: Make the scene safe for you and the child

steps.label: Responsive?
steps.sub: Voice and touch; no painful stimuli

steps.label: Airway + breathing
steps.sub: Head tilt chin lift; look up to 10 s

steps.label: 5 rescue breaths
steps.sub: About 1 s each, chest visibly rises

teach.caption: Second rescuer: call and bring an AED. Single rescuer: calling and starting CPR come before fetching an AED. Without a phone, do 1 minute of CPR before going for help.

rows.label: Depth
values: At least one third of chest depth
At least one third; 5–6 cm in adolescents

teach.caption: Compress the lower half of the sternum at 100–120 per minute, let the chest recoil fully, and do not exceed 6 cm at any age.
25 kg is about 8 years. If the AED has no paediatric setting, use it in standard adult mode.

teach.body: Call for help as soon as you detect deterioration: do not wait for an arrest. If arrest is suspected, one person calls the resuscitation team while another starts CPR at 15:2. Competent staff use bag-mask ventilation with oxygen. If ventilation cannot start straight away, begin compressions and add breaths as soon as possible. Pads for children under 25 kg go anteroposterior: front mid-chest left of the sternum, back between the shoulder blades.

root.label: Suspected choking
root.sub: Cannot speak, cry aloud or cough well

children.label: Up to 5 back blows, then up to 5 thrusts
children.sub: Infant: chest thrusts. Child: abdominal thrusts

items: Infant: face down along your forearm, resting on your leg, head lower than chest; sharp blows between the shoulder blades.
Child: lean them forward and give blows between the shoulder blades.
Infant chest thrusts: on their back on your knees, two-thumb encircling, sharper than compressions.
Child abdominal thrusts: fist between navel and xiphoid, pull sharply inwards and upwards.
Stop as soon as there are signs of relief: coughing, loud breathing or crying.

teach.text: Abdominal thrusts are not used in infants: give chest thrusts with the two-thumb technique instead. And do not blind finger sweep; remove an object with a single sweep only if it is clearly visible.

teach.body: Nurse Gemma finds Ivy unresponsive, not breathing normally. Ivy's mother has the ambulance on speaker. Gemma opens the airway with the head neutral, checks breathing for no more than 10 seconds, gives 5 rescue breaths over Ivy's mouth and nose, watching for chest rise, then starts two-thumb encircling compressions at 15:2 because she is trained in PBLS.

items: Check responsiveness by voice and touch; call the ambulance on speaker.
Breathing check no more than 10 s, then 5 rescue breaths.
15:2 if PBLS-trained, 30:2 if not; two-thumb encircling in all infants.
AED: paediatric mode under 25 kg (about 8 years); single rescuer calls and starts CPR before fetching it.
Choking: up to 5 back blows then up to 5 thrusts (chest in infants, abdominal in children); no blind sweeps.

summary: You can now deliver paediatric BLS to RCUK 2025, including 5 rescue breaths, the right ratio for your training and the correct compression technique and AED mode. You can also manage choking in infants and children, conscious or unconscious.

A.q: A community children's nurse trained in PBLS finds Ivy, 4 months, unresponsive and not breathing normally. The ambulance has been called. What should the nurse do next?
A.why: RCUK 2025: after opening the airway and checking breathing, give 5 initial rescue breaths, then start compressions.

whyNot.0: Children usually arrest from hypoxia, so the 5 rescue breaths come before compressions.
whyNot.2: A single rescuer prioritises calling and starting CPR over fetching an AED.
whyNot.3: Paediatric BLS starts with 5 rescue breaths, and a PBLS-trained nurse uses 15:2.

A.q: Which compression technique does RCUK 2025 recommend for infants?
options: Two fingers on the lower sternum
Two hands, one on the other
A.why: RCUK 2025 recommends the two-thumb encircling technique for chest compressions in all infants.

whyNot.0: The two-finger technique was replaced by two-thumb encircling in 2025.
whyNot.1: One hand is used in children over 1 year.
whyNot.3: Two hands are used in larger children and adolescents.

A.q: Ella, 9 months, is choking on a piece of apple. She is conscious but her cough is no longer effective. What should the nurse do first?
options: Sweep her mouth with a finger
A.why: If coughing is ineffective, give up to 5 back blows with the infant face down along the forearm, head lower than the chest.

whyNot.1: Abdominal thrusts are not used in infants; chest thrusts follow back blows.
whyNot.2: Blind finger sweeps are not done; a single sweep is used for a clearly visible object.
whyNot.3: Rescue breaths start when the infant becomes unconscious.

B.q: Noah, 6, collapses on a children's ward and is not breathing. Two registered nurses trained in PBLS respond. What ratio should they use?
B.why: In hospital, and for anyone trained in PBLS, the compression-to-ventilation ratio is 15:2.

whyNot.1: 30:2 is for untrained bystanders or those trained only in adult BLS.
whyNot.2: 5:1 is not an RCUK paediatric ratio.
whyNot.3: 3:1 is used in newborn life support, not paediatric BLS.

B.q: Leo, 5, is choking on a sweet. He is conscious but cannot speak or cough. Five back blows have not worked. What next?
options: Lie him down for rescue breaths
B.why: In a conscious child, if back blows fail, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts, then alternate with back blows.

whyNot.0: Chest thrusts are for infants under 1 year.
whyNot.1: Back blows alternate with abdominal thrusts rather than being repeated alone.
whyNot.2: Rescue breaths start when the child becomes unconscious.

B.q: Mason, 6, weighs 21 kg and is in cardiac arrest. An AED arrives. How should it be used?
options: Paediatric mode, pads on the left chest
B.why: Under 25 kg: activate paediatric mode if available and place pads anteroposterior (front mid-chest left of the sternum, back between the scapulae).

whyNot.0: Adult mode is for children over 25 kg, or when no paediatric mode exists.
whyNot.1: Both pads on the front risk them touching in a small child; anteroposterior is advised under 25 kg.
whyNot.3: An AED can be used safely in children; waiting delays defibrillation.

C.q: Isla, 10 months, has been choking on a grape. After two rounds of back blows and chest thrusts she becomes limp and unresponsive. The ambulance is on its way. What should the nurse do?
options: Continue back blows with her on her back
Turn her into the recovery position
Do a finger sweep of the back of her throat
Begin CPR, starting with 5 rescue breaths
C.why: RCUK 2025: when a choking child becomes unconscious, start CPR immediately with 5 rescue breaths.

whyNot.0: Back blows stop once the infant is unconscious; CPR begins.
whyNot.1: Recovery position is for an unresponsive child who is breathing effectively.
whyNot.2: Blind finger sweeps can push the object further in.

C.q: A children's nurse is alone in a park, without a phone, when Amir, 7, collapses and is not breathing normally. What is the correct order?
options: Go for help first, then return to start CPR
Do 1 minute of CPR, then go for help
Find an AED, then start CPR
Give 5 breaths, then go for help
C.why: RCUK 2025: a single rescuer without a mobile phone should perform CPR for 1 minute before going to seek help.

whyNot.0: Leaving at once means no oxygen delivery while help is sought.
whyNot.2: A single rescuer prioritises CPR over fetching an AED.
whyNot.3: Rescue breaths without compressions are not a full minute of CPR.

C.q: A healthcare assistant trained only in adult BLS is helping with CPR on a 4-year-old outside hospital. What ratio is correct for her?
C.why: RCUK 2025: untrained or adult-trained rescuers use 30:2, still starting with 5 initial rescue breaths.

whyNot.0: 15:2 is for those specifically trained in PBLS.
whyNot.1: The 5 initial rescue breaths are given whatever the rescuer's training.
whyNot.3: Compression-only CPR is for rescuers unwilling or unable to give breaths.

reteach.title: Breathe first, then pump
reteach.question: Why does paediatric BLS start with breaths when adult BLS starts with compressions?

blocks.h: Children run out of oxygen first
blocks.body: In adults, sudden arrest is often a heart rhythm problem, so compressions come first. Children usually arrest after a period of poor breathing or shock, so their blood is already short of oxygen. Five rescue breaths top up the oxygen before compressions circulate it. Then keep going at 15:2 if you are PBLS-trained, or 30:2 if not.

blocks.text: Ratios depend on training, not the child's age: a PBLS-trained nurse uses 15:2 for an infant or a teenager; an untrained bystander uses 30:2.

explain.body: Check responsiveness by voice and touch, not pain. Call the ambulance on speaker. Open the airway (neutral in infants) and look for normal breathing and signs of life for no more than 10 seconds.

test.q: How should responsiveness be checked in paediatric BLS?
test.why: RCUK 2025: use verbal and tactile stimulation; do not use painful stimuli.

whyNot.0: A sternal rub is a painful stimulus.
whyNot.1: A trapezius squeeze is a painful stimulus.
whyNot.3: Nail bed pressure is a painful stimulus.

explain.body: Give 5 rescue breaths, each about 1 second, enough to make the chest rise. Then 15:2 if PBLS-trained, 30:2 otherwise.

test.q: How long should each rescue breath last?
test.why: Each breath should be given steadily over about 1 second, enough to make the chest visibly rise.

whyNot.1: 3 seconds is too long and delays compressions.
whyNot.2: Half a second is too short to inflate the chest effectively.

explain.body: Lower half of the sternum, at least one third of chest depth, 100–120 per minute, full recoil, not more than 6 cm. AED paediatric mode under 25 kg; pads anteroposterior.

test.q: What is the maximum compression depth at any age?
test.why: RCUK 2025: do not exceed a compression depth of 6 cm at any age.

whyNot.0: 4 cm is not the stated limit; depth is at least one third of the chest.
whyNot.1: 5 cm is the lower end of the adolescent range, not the maximum.

explain.body: Effective cough: encourage it. Ineffective: up to 5 back blows, then up to 5 chest thrusts (infant) or abdominal thrusts (child), alternating. Unconscious: CPR starting with 5 breaths.

test.q: When should back blows and thrusts stop in a conscious choking child?
options: When the child starts to turn pale
test.why: Stop as soon as there are signs of relief such as coughing, loud breathing or crying.

whyNot.0: There is no set number of cycles; continue until relieved or unconscious.
whyNot.1: Continue until relief or unconsciousness, not until the crew arrives.
